newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-FORMER CHAMPION PIERCE BATTLES HER WAY INTO LAST FOUR.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-FORMER CHAMPION PIERCE BATTLES HER WAY INTO LAST FOUR.

text.p: Former champion Mary Pierce showed rare self-belief on Tuesday as she fought back against Belgium's Sabine Appelmans to win a place in the Australian Open semifinals.
France's Pierce, winner here in 1995, lost the first set 6-1 before levelling the match in the second and then came back from 3-0 down in the third to beat the 16th seeded Appelmans 1-6 6-4 6-4.
"That's the great thing about tennis, you never know what's going to happen," she said, looking forward to a tough semifinal date with South Africa's Amanda Coetzer.
In earlier matches unseeded Spaniard Carlos Moya beat his friend and Barcelona training partner Felix Mantilla in four sets and Coetzer, the number 12 seed, brushed aside American Kimberly Po.
The day-time session was overshadowed, however, by a row over the tournament referee's decision to pull the roof over Centre Court to spare players and public from a heatwave.
Courtside temperatures at Melbourne Park exceeded 50 degrees Celsius over the weekend, contributing to a seed's collapse and provoking warnings that players could be at risk.

But referee Peter Bellenger's decision to close out the sun provoked an angry reaction among players, coaches and tennis veterans who said Melbourne's fickle weather was part of the tournament's tradition.
"I was going to play anyway so even if it's snowing, raining or 60 degrees (Celsius), I don't care," Moya told reporters after beating fellow Spaniard Felix Mantilla in four sets.
"I think it may have been a different match in the sun and wind," retorted a furious Mantilla.
Moya had to put friendship aside as he disposed of 14th-seeded Mantilla 7-5 6-2 6-7 6-2 in two hours 29 minutes.

Once considered just another Spanish clay-court baseliner, Moya has grown in confidence since ousting defending champion Boris Becker in the first round. On Tuesday he regularly came forward to the net.
"Felix does not make stupid mistakes, so if you want to beat him you have to take risks," he said.
It was Spain's best performance at the Australian Open since Andres Gimeno lost the 1969 final to Australian Rod Laver.
Moya's semifinal opponent will be either world number two Michael Chang of the United States or Chilean danger man Marcelo Rios, the ninth seed. The two men were playing later on Tuesday.
In the first women's quarter-final, Coetzer showed the same form which helped her bring down top seed Steffi Graf as she beat Po 6-4 6-1 in a match lasting 67 minutes.
Coetzer is seen as the player with the best chance of beating Swiss starlet Martina Hingis if both win through to Saturday's final. Her performance on Tuesday could only have reinforced that view.
Although Po managed to break Coetzer's serve once in each set, the South African converted six of six break points.
Coetzer also criticised the decision to shut the roof for the day's play, although she conceded it had given her and Po a break from the heat.
"I definitely would have preferred playing outside...I love playing out in the sun," she said.
Since her victory here in 1995, Pierce has had to cope with a prolonged form slump and a shoulder injury, a combination which prompted her to take a three-month break from the game late last year.
She has showed a new positive attitude since her return, winning two of her matches in Melbourne despite going a set down and playing some typically aggressive tennis.
"A year or two ago I probably would have lost this match," she said on Tuesday.
Appelmans, more excited at having reached the quarter-finals than distressed at her defeat, said she thought Pierce had the ability to win the tournament again.
"Every match she's been improving, she's playing better. She has a good chance if she can keep it up and believe in herself."
